Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
items.summary:
How Meta's Reality Labs brought Cuttlefish and its QEMU backend to macOS and Apple silicon. [...]

Read More...

The post Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses. Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware.

Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware.

Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does.

Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side.

We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS.

The Impact of Fragmentation

Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux.

The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation.

The Stack and the macOS Gaps

Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time. To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support.

Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three.

Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux

The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user, and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux.

Living Within Hypervisor.framework

On Apple silicon, QEMU accelerates through HVF (Hypervisor.framework) instead of KVM. QEMU’s HVF backend did not track enough memory regions for larger Cuttlefish configurations. We increased its tracking-slot count so those configurations could run correctly.

A Usable Native Display

Local application development requires an interactive display allowing developers to view and engage directly with the virtual device. To enable direct interaction and bypass reliance on the WebRTC interface, we transitioned to QEMU’s native Cocoa display. The changes include:

  • BGRA Pixel Format Support: Enables accurate display rendering to eliminate visual artifacts on Apple silicon.
  • Mouse-Click-as-Touch: Translates pointer actions into touch input for interacting with touchscreen devices.
  • Custom Geometry Options: Adds the -g flag to graphic_console_init for display configuration.

We also enabled the unstable Rutabaga structs needed to match the Rust-side graphics ABI in gfxstream/rutabaga configurations.

Building and Signing on Apple Silicon

Finally, there was the build and packaging work: initial Darwin build support, building QEMU for arm64 on macOS, and toolchain fixes. The macOS builds also needed the JIT entitlement in addition to support for code signing and notarization. On the Cuttlefish side, we added macOS host support so the framework’s orchestration builds and runs on a Mac instead of assuming a Linux host.

The Benefits

By moving to a unified platform, we cut maintenance requirements, reduced infrastructure needs, eliminated redundant tooling, enhanced fidelity, and ensured developers run the exact same Cuttlefish virtual devices used across CI.

A single platform also made it easier to support capabilities on a shared stack, including:

  • Bluetooth pairing and connectivity.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Cellular.
  • 3D graphics.
  • Over-the-air (OTA) update testing to exercise over-the-air update flows against a virtual device.
  • Fastboot.
  • Snapshotting to save and restore device state in CI and development flows.

Beyond supporting Reality Labs engineers, this identical virtual device is shared with external developers building for our ecosystem. This alignment guarantees that third-party teams test against the exact same Cuttlefish-based platform we use to develop and validate the OS itself.

With AI agents playing a growing role in Android development, validation execution and runtime behavior is just as essential as code generation. Virtual devices empower both engineers and automated agents to operate concurrently within isolated environments, facilitating application execution and rapid iteration. By enabling instant state resets and repeated test runs, teams eliminate dependencies on shared physical hardware and prevent workflow interruptions. Ultimately, high-fidelity emulation ensures these continuous feedback loops are both rapid and meaningful.

Giving Back to the Community

Although we built this for development within Reality Labs, the macOS support is useful beyond our products. We’re sharing our work with the community so other developers can build on the QEMU and AOSP foundations that enabled our work.

We’re distributing the work in two parts:

  • qemu-wearables: a Meta-maintained fork of QEMU carrying our commits.
  • cuttlefish-wearables: a set of patch files, with instructions for patching Android/AOSP.

The repositories contain our QEMU changes and the Cuttlefish patch series, along with build and patch-application instructions.

We’re also exploring ways to contribute these changes upstream to QEMU and AOSP. In the meantime, developers can use our fork and patch set.

Acknowledgements

This project relies on the foundations laid by the QEMU and Cuttlefish/AOSP communities. We are particularly grateful for the vsock-user implementation created by Stefano Garzarella, which directly enabled our macOS integration.

Special thanks also go to Olya Arkhangelskaia and Tom Care at Meta for their foundational work bringing Cuttlefish to macOS, and to Jeffrey Effendy for improvements to the native Mac developer experience and subsequent productization work.

items.title: LangChain Raises $300M to Enable Every Company to Own Its Intelligence
items.summary:
Our Series C Announcement

Today, we’re announcing that LangChain raised $300M at a $3B valuation to advance our mission to enable every company to own its intelligence. The round was led by existing investor CapitalG, with significant participation from new investors GIC and DFJ Growth and existing investors IVP and Sapphire Ventures.

We believe agents will transform the economy. That future will be shaped by domain-specific agents differentiated by their knowledge, data, and UX. These agents will be sold as standalone products and also used to transform internal company operations. The companies that control these systems will build lasting competitive advantages.

To capture that opportunity, every company will need to own its intelligence. Companies should be free to choose the best models for their needs, control their data and infrastructure, and continuously improve their agents, while maintaining the governance needed to operate securely at scale.

That’s why we’ve built LangSmith, the framework-agnostic platform to run, improve, and govern agents. More than 7,000 organizations already rely on LangSmith, from fast-growing startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Listen Labs to Fortune 500 enterprises like NVIDIA, Toyota, and Salesforce. Clay uses LangSmith to monitor hundreds of millions of agent runs per month and improve their agents. Workday uses LangSmith to run and govern agents across the organization, reducing the time to deploy a new agent from five months to under a day.

LangSmith provides the foundation for companies to control their agent systems across three pillars – Agent Runtime, Agent Improvement, and Agent Governance:

Agent Runtime gives teams the architecture and infrastructure to run agents reliably. Deep Agents, LangGraph, and LangChain give developers flexibility across models and control over how context is managed. LangSmith Agent Server and Sandboxes allow teams to deploy and run agents securely at scale, whether in the cloud or in their environment. LangSmith Managed Agents and Fleet provide fully managed services to build, deploy, and run mission-critical agents in production.

Agent Improvement helps teams test, monitor, and improve agent performance. LangSmith Observability and Evaluation give teams visibility into how agents behave and measure quality. LangSmith Engine, our in-platform agent, automates improvement by finding errors, writing code and prompt fixes, and monitoring production traffic for regressions. LangSmith Fine-Tuning helps teams turn agent traces into training data to fine-tune and evaluate specialized models.

Agent Governance gives teams centralized control over how agents use models, tools, and data. Our LLM and Tool Gateways help teams manage model budgets and fallbacks, protect sensitive data, and govern tool access and authentication across teams and agents.

Next Friday, November 20th, we’ll share several new LangSmith capabilities that build on this foundation. Join us for a special release event to see what’s coming next.

LangSmith has been shaped by our fantastic community – from our developer evangelists to the customers we’re lucky enough to partner with. Thank you all for your feedback, insights, and trust.

There’s still so much left to build. Building high performing agents is harder than it should be, and we‘re determined to change that. Come join us in making it easier for every company to own its intelligence.

Harrison

‍

Thank you to our new and existing investors for helping make this journey possible. We’re excited to welcome Salesforce Ventures, Insight Venture Partners, QuantumLight, and MongoDB Ventures, and grateful to Sequoia, Amplify, and Benchmark for doubling down in this round.

How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
items.summary: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients.  Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI […]
items.content:
From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. 

Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications.

Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care.

Friday, Nov. 13, 5:00 a.m. PT

Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care 

Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts. 

Dyania Health, a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. 

The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. 

Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls

Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall.  The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. 

Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. 

Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. 

Synapsis AI in the Real World

Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. 

Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand. 

“Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson, chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic.

The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries.

Learn more about Dyania Health.

items.title: BRQGen: Towards Adaptive Completeness Assessment and Follow-Up Question Generation for Bug Reports
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15903v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many bug reports lack the necessary information required to reproduce issues. In early studies, large language models have been employed to generate follow-up questions to enhance incomplete reports. However, they ask a fixed number of questions regardless of whether the report is incomplete. We propose BRQGen, an iterative framework that identifies missing or ambiguous information in bug reports and generates targeted follow-up questions, only if necessary. Reports with no identified gaps are classified as sufficient. When the author responds, BRQGen evaluates whether the answers provide the requested information and generates further questions for any exposed gaps. We curated a novel dataset of 429 incomplete bug reports from Home Assistant and Brave Browser, each containing at least one maintainer follow-up question. Each question is mapped to the author's answer and assigned a label indicating whether the requested information could have been provided directly through the issue template. Earlier maintainer requests were associated with author responses, whereas delayed requests were associated with no response. Among responding authors, requests within one hour received median replies after 0.52 hours in Home Assistant and 1.45 hours in Brave, versus 9.76 and 13.49 hours after four hours. BRQGen covered 35.4% (Qwen 3.8 Flash) to 51.8% (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) of the 1,073 ground-truth follow-up questions. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash managed to ask 45.7% of all detailed questions and 63.9% of all generic questions. Gemini 3 Flash Preview reached the highest macro-F1 for completeness assessment of 49.3%, but with a post-hoc analysis by getting only the gaps with high severities, Qwen 3.8 Flash reaches 73.6% macro-F1 score. Completeness assessment improved when at least one identified gap had high severity, and nearly all ground-truth questions were captured within the first two iterations.
items.author: Tevfik Emre Sungur, Akif Emre K\"o\c{s}\"u\c{s}, U\u{g}urcan Do\u{g}ru\c{c}am, Eray T\"uz\"un

items.title: The Import Tax: A Longitudinal Measurement of Startup Cost in the Python Ecosystem
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.02753v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Python programs pay for their imports at every process start, a cost that is invisible in steady-state benchmarks but dominant for command-line tools, test workers, and serverless cold starts. Python 3.15 adds explicit lazy imports (PEP 810) on largely anecdotal evidence. We measure the import cost of the 500 most-downloaded PyPI packages, every quarterly release since mid-2021, under six CPython versions (3.9-3.14) on two platforms (Apple M5/macOS and Intel Xeon/Linux), 66,816 cells in all, with targeted experiments that isolate individual effects. Values are for macOS (Linux in parentheses). Import cost is heavily skewed (median 12.3 ms, 99th percentile 400 ms). Among packages that import in more than 2 ms, namespace distributions excluded, the median package spends 68% of its import time in the standard library (68% on Linux with the interpreter on local storage, 79% on network storage). Precompiling bytecode removes almost all of the cold-start penalty on Linux and 92% of it for the median package on macOS, but only a third of the summed macOS penalty: packages with native libraries pay a security assessment of each library that the system has not seen before, again in every fresh environment. A package's own import code grows by a median 4.0% (5.0%) per year; installing each release with the dependencies of its time changes its trend by a median of only 0.15 (0.35) percentage points (CPython 3.9). CPython 3.14 runs package code faster than 3.9 but imports more and slower standard-library modules, a net 1.16x (1.07x) slowdown. Submodules that dependents import beyond the top level add nothing for the median package and at most 11.7 (49.5) ms for nine packages in ten. On CPython 3.15, global lazy mode cuts the imports that dependents perform to 0.41x (0.39x) of their cost, and 38 of 461 packages fail under it, many only on first use of a name. Harness, code, and dataset are public.
items.author: Trinath Sai Subhash Reddy Pittala

items.title: SACS: A Code Smell Dataset using Semi-automatic Generation Approach
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.15342v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Code smell is a great challenge in software refactoring, which indicates latent design or implementation flaws that may degrade the software maintainability and evolution. Over the past of decades, the research on code smell has received extensive attention. Especially the researches applied machine learning-technique have become a popular topic in recent studies. However, one of the biggest challenges to apply machine learning-technique is the lack of high-quality code smell datasets. Manually constructing such datasets is extremely labor-intensive, as identifying code smells requires substantial development expertise and considerable time investment. In contrast, automatically generated datasets, while scalable, frequently exhibit reduced label reliability and compromised data quality. To overcome this challenge, in this study, we explore a semi-automatic approach to generate a code smell dataset with high quality data samples. Specifically, we first applied a set of automatic generation rules to produce candidate smelly samples. We then employed multiple metrics to group the data samples into an automatically accepted group and a manually reviewed group, enabling reviewers to concentrate their efforts on ambiguous samples. Furthermore, we established structured review guidelines and developed a annotation tool to support the manual validation process. Based on the proposed semi-automatic generation approach, we created an open-source code smell dataset, SACS, covering three widely studied code smells: Long Method, Large Class, and Feature Envy. Each code smell category includes over 10,000 labeled samples. This dataset could provide a large-scale and publicly available benchmark to facilitate future studies on code smell detection and automated refactoring.
items.author: Hanyu Zhang, Tomoji Kishi

items.title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.18594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.
items.author: Tobias H\"urten, Johannes F. Loevenich, Florian Spelter, Erik Adler, Laurin Holz, Maxime Schwarzer, Thies Moehlenhof, Roberto Rigolin F. Lopes

items.title: Small area learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a novel learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop estimators with and without cross-fitting, accommodating low-complexity and flexible learners and unifying synthetic, model-based, and semi-supervised estimators. For area means, we establish a unified asymptotic theory for these estimator families, characterizing conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality and providing variance estimators and confidence intervals without prescribing a particular learning algorithm. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals clearly a bias-variance trade-off: partial residual correction in classical estimators can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to the misspecification of working models, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34%-49% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.
items.author: Katarzyna Reluga, Nicola Salvati, Setareh Ranjbar, Nikos Tzavidis, Mark van der Laan

items.title: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.14894v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/xuzhikangnba/torch-tvae.
items.author: Zhikang Xu, Jiarui Xing, Jian Wang

items.title: Rethinking Floorplan Generation with Space Syntax: From Design Theory to Model Improvement
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.22507v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Architectural design increasingly adopts generative AI (GenAI) for floorplan generation, an early-stage design task exploring how spaces should be organized for use. Yet fidelity objectives inherited from native visual and geometric generators do not automatically capture this design purpose. This organization remains largely implicit in generated representations, limiting direct evaluation and feedback. Drawing on space syntax, an established architectural design theory, the Space Syntax Integration Operator (SSIO) recovers convex-space access graphs across heterogeneous formats. This theory-grounded shared intermediate representation, which we call a design container, supports evaluation and model understanding of spatial design. Applying SSIO to four residential corpora spanning 15 countries reveals public spaces' integration levels are highest, with corpus-dependent distributions. These patterns underpin the RPLAN-SSI benchmark, an empirical design reference system assessing population-level functional-profile alignment (IPD) and distributional alignment of within-plan public-space advantage (PIAD). Comparison with this residential reference reveals a design gap: public spaces in generated floorplans have a smaller integration advantage over other spaces. To address this gap, Space Syntax-Guided Post-Training (SSPT) provides a plug-and-play design-learning interface: SSIO-derived RL feedback reduces IPD and PIAD across five heterogeneous diffusion backbones while preserving native mechanisms. We further discuss how this approach may inform GenAI applications in other design domains.
items.author: Zhuoyang Jiang, Dongqing Zhang, Qingxiang Liu, Yuxuan Liang

items.title: Governing Copyright Responsibly in the Era of Generative AI
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.17002v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, while authors generally lack work-level information about whether and how their works were used. This paper asks how copyright governance frames and operationalises the protection of such authors, and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026 were coded deductively against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. The European Union and the United States are the primary cases; the United Kingdom, China and international bodies serve as comparators. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, while reflexivity is the least represented category and reaches its minimum in the US sub-corpus. Both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training. From the coded gaps, the paper derives a six-instrument governance design and a capacity-based allocation of responsibility among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.
items.author: D. Kochetkov

items.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16837v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
items.author: Pengcheng Wang, Zhexuan Zhang, Chao Lou, Kewei Tu

items.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.16102v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tacit knowing is an operating regime of one memory substrate, not a separate kind of content. In VaCoAl (CASRAM, PyVaCoAl), an algebro-deterministic hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), one DAG of bound records is read in two ways. With every collision repaired (Rescue), the trace is exactly auditable but no path outranks another; with collisions tolerated (Don't Care), a path-integrated confidence $CR_2$ ranks direct over circuitous routes without being stated. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding. (2) Full explication destroys the valuation (Lemma 1), as with Polanyi's pianist; tacitness is contingent or regime-bound, placing Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins on one substrate. (3) The same lemma answers the popular dual-process moral ("train slow System 2 to tame fast System 1"), which mirrors the two-store reading of knowledge Polanyi rejected; Mercier and Sperber's reply, that reasoning is intuitive inference about reasons, matches his. (4) To know a large DAG is to cull it. Simon answered Polanyi's Meno argument: a test and a generator suffice. The AlphaGo-to-AlphaProof lineage builds that answer, yet a checker audits an endpoint and values no path: the tacit is relocated, not removed, and results are verified yet rootless. (5) Collins's three tacit knowledges map to bound structure, substrate valuation and value binding. (6) Our mentor-student DAG charts tacit transmission. (7) AI-solved problems with few follow-ups (Tao) are rootless explicit knowledge, re-rooted when LLMs generate, VaCoAl keeps the trace and the community values. (8) On Mercier and Sperber's theory an LLM is a sophist; truth-seeking lies in collective tacit knowing, Polanyi's conviviality, which we conjecture extends beyond humans. Testable predictions follow.
items.author: Hiroyuki Chuma, Kanji Otsuka, Yoichi Sato, Kodo Yamauchi

items.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15221v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.
items.author: Zhaoyuan Qiu, Sachith Seneviratne, Yu Xia, Saman Halgamuge

items.title: Four conditions for composing plugin-based agents without a host agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.28553v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model agents now run long-horizon, multi-tool, autonomous sessions, and the infrastructure must keep the current assembly of capabilities, the progress of execution, and the basis for recovery after a fault. A single-process host holds this information in its own running state, so its death takes the session record and the assembly with it. This paper gives four conditions under which a plugin-based agent needs no host process, one each on state placement, record carriers, recovery coordination, and provider resolution. The store, writer, and delivery disciplines keep the conditions in force, and each carries formal support from the spatiotemporal-composability calculus and from the proofs in the supplementary materials. An agent that meets them can be constructed with its assembly on a bus of peer processes and its record in an append-only carrier owned by no process, and removing any one part makes the assembly need a host again. The conditions themselves are the contribution, and every implementation that meets them inherits the same advantages. Such an agent keeps its session through the death of any process, wastes no calls after a fault, loses no records, recovers locally, changes its capability set while it runs, and carries its undo semantics across processes. This paper builds one SDK of the conditions, Logos, and measures whether it fulfills their promise against the single-process reference and a configuration over MCP under one fault in each of 200 tasks, realized in 197. The reference lost all 197 faulted sessions, the MCP configuration kept its sessions but issued 1,212 wasted calls, and the SDK kept every session, wasted no call, lost no record, and fulfilled the promise of the conditions in every faulted task, with task performance preserved. The conditions give builders a tested route from single-process hosts to peer processes.
items.author: Hanzhang Jia, Liheng Zeng, Hao Cheng, Yi Gao, Bo Ma, Guolong Xu

items.title: ASAP: Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode Refinement For Binary Decompilation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.06900v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in binary decompilation to refine the C-like pseudocode produced by traditional rule-based decompilers. While this pseudocode is useful, it is a heuristic and lossy abstraction rather than a faithful copy of the source code. It often contains decompiler errors, especially for aggressively optimized binaries where critical low-level details are obscured. We present ASAP, an Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode refinement framework for binary decompilation. ASAP learns source-aligned assembly representations from paired source and binary functions using joint function-level and snippet-level contrastive alignment. A Q-Former then compresses chunk-level assembly features into a fixed number of assembly tokens. These tokens and the decompiler-produced pseudocode jointly condition the decompilation LLM. During refinement, we use stochastic pseudocode masking and a relative assembly-advantage loss to discourage the model from relying solely on pseudocode. On two decompilation benchmarks across multiple compiler optimization levels, ASAP improves the average re-execution rate from 64.7% to 71.9% and the average recompilation rate from 91.6% to 96.6% compared with the strongest baseline. Our approach offers both a new perspective and a practical solution to binary decompilation.
items.author: Yujian Zhuang, Dehong Gao, Qichao Zhang, Qijing Lai, Jiaxin Wang, Libin Yang, Xiaoyan Cai

items.title: Scentree: a framework for generating scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.21495v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We present scentree, an open-source Python package for constructing scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming models using either historical data or samples drawn from a probability distribution. It combines machine learning and multivariate time series models to obtain a scenario fan that captures dependencies in the stochastic processes. This scenario fan is subsequently reduced into a scenario tree that preserves representativeness of the stochastic process, providing a flexible and extensible framework for uncertainty modeling in stochastic programming problems. The framework can also be naturally applied to two-stage stochastic programming problems. Key contributions are the joint modeling of the stochastic process, preserving correlations between all random variables, and the automation of the complete workflow, including forecasting model selection, parameter estimation, scenario fan generation, and scenario tree construction. In addition, scentree does not assume any underlying data distribution, reducing the statistical expertise required to produce a scenario tree, and is modular by design, allowing external forecasts and other partial executions of the workflow.
items.author: Cristian Pach\'on-Garc\'ia, Albert Sol\`a Vilalta, F. -Javier Heredia

items.title: Insights from GitHub Community on the Matter Standard: Developer Perspectives and Challenges
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.01494v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Matter seeks to resolve longstanding interoperability problems in the Internet of Things (IoT), yet little is known about how developers experience the standard in day to day work. This paper examines over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository to understand the kinds of problems contributors report when implementing and integrating Matter. Using topic modeling and qualitative analysis, we identify four recurring areas of concern, Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform and Network, and describe how they manifest in the evolution of the codebase and tooling. The findings reveal systematic technical and integration challenges and point to concrete opportunities to refine Matter's test infrastructure, cross vendor guidance, and documentation as the standard continues to mature.
items.author: Muhammad Hassan, Carl Gunter, Susan Landau, Masooda Bashir

items.title: Automated Code Review Assignments: An Alternative Perspective of Code Ownership on GitHub
items.summary:
arXiv:2512.05551v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Code ownership is central to ensuring accountability and maintaining quality in large-scale software development. Yet, as software supply chain attacks threaten project health and quality assurance, mechanisms for assigning and enforcing responsibility have become critical. In 2017, GitHub introduced the CODEOWNERS feature, a file in the repository that names the developers responsible for specific files and automatically requests them as reviewers, to strengthen accountability and protect critical parts of the codebase. Little is known about how CODEOWNERS is adopted and practiced. We present the first large-scale empirical study of CODEOWNERS usage across over 844,000 pull requests with 1.9 million comments and over 2 million reviews. We identify 10,287 designated owners, the developers named in CODEOWNERS files, track their code review activities, and compare them with contribution-based owners, the developers who contributed at least 5% of a file's lines. Results indicate that designated owners take part in a moderate share of the pull requests that touch their files, that their collaborative behavior resembles that of contribution-based owners, and that after adoption merge time and review effort grow more slowly, or fall, relative to their pre-adoption trend. Using regression discontinuity design analysis, we further find that designated owners' review, decision (approval and merge), and authoring activity jumps upward at adoption, and that over the following year they do more review and decision work per pull request than before, whereas contribution-based owners do less review work per pull request. Our results position CODEOWNERS as a promising yet sparsely adopted mechanism for improving software governance and resilience. We discuss how projects can leverage this alternative ownership method to enhance security and accountability in open-source development.
items.author: Jai Lal Lulla, Raula Gaikovina Kula, Christoph Treude

items.title: Architectural Degradation: Definition, Motivations, Measurement and Remediation Approaches
items.summary:
arXiv:2507.14547v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Architectural degradation, also known as erosion, decay, or aging, impacts system quality, maintainability, and adaptability. Although widely acknowledged, current literature shows fragmented definitions, metrics, and remediation strategies. Our study aims to unify understanding of architectural degradation by identifying its definitions, causes, metrics, tools, and remediation approaches across academic and gray literature. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 108 studies extracting definitions, causes, metrics, measurement approaches, tools, and remediation strategies. We developed a taxonomy encompassing architectural, code, and process debt to explore definition evolution, methodological trends, and research gaps. Architectural degradation has shifted from a low-level issue to a socio-technical concern. Definitions now address code violations, design drift, and structural decay. Causes fall under architectural (e.g., poor documentation), code (e.g., hasty fixes), and process debt (e.g., knowledge loss). We identified 54 metrics and 31 measurement techniques, focused on smells, cohesion/coupling, and evolution. Yet, most tools detect issues but rarely support ongoing or preventive remediation. Degradation is both technical and organizational. While detection is well-studied, continuous remediation remains lacking. Our study reveals missed integration between metrics, tools, and repair logic, urging holistic, proactive strategies for sustainable architecture.
items.author: Noman Ahmad, Ruoyu Su, Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Valentina Lenarduzzi, Davide Taibi

items.title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17123v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.
items.author: Zhezhen Cao, Weiyuan Ding, Bowen Xu

items.title: A Code-Level Audit of X
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16800v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The transparency regime of recommender systems on Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) is undergoing significant change under the EU Digital Services Act (DSA). The DSA requires platforms to disclose information about their recommendation pipelines and grants vetted researchers access to non-public data, which may extend to recommender code. However, it is not known to what extent such code releases enable substantive and meaningful third-party auditing of a production recommender system. We address this question by proposing a code-level audit methodology for recommender systems and applying it to the X platform, which has voluntarily open-sourced its recommender pipeline. Our methodology is a backwards-walk traversal of the repository, tracing each decision-relevant component from the user-facing timeline back to its upstream producers, checking that it is reachable from the served pipeline, and classifying each under a four-tier inspectability scheme. Applying this procedure, we identify 13 transparency dead-ends on the live serving path: models, services, label lists, and configuration values that the public code depends on but the release does not contain. We find that the components that decide which posts are filtered and how they are ranked fall into the two least inspectable tiers, a pattern that intensifies with the 2025 integration of the proprietary Grok language model into moderation, annotation, and ranking. We further show that the release keeps 2023 code that the 2025 pipeline no longer reaches, with 36 parameter references that would pass for dead-ends without a reachability check. Finally, we discuss which additional artifacts would be required for meaningful auditing.
items.author: Luka Bekavac, Simon Mayer

items.title: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Cross-Version PoC Migration in Python Web Applications
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16588v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Affected-version ranges in vulnerability databases decide which deployments scanners, patching pipelines, and incident responders treat as vulnerable, yet these ranges are often incomplete, so vulnerable releases are silently treated as safe. Auditing them requires executable evidence: given a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a listed version, show that the same vulnerability can be triggered on an earlier, unlisted version. This cross-version PoC migration combines source-code analysis, environment repair, and execution-based verification. We introduce CrossPloit, a benchmark of 127 migration instances across 45 CVEs in the Python web ecosystem. Each instance includes a version-pinned container, a reference PoC, and a vulnerability-specific oracle; two validators check that the observed effect arises from the disclosed vulnerability. Benchmark construction confirms 149 vulnerable prior versions absent from the affected-version lists of four databases, 127 of which require migration. Across 18 agent configurations (nine models and two harnesses), the best configuration resolves 58.3% of instances, compared with 8.7% for an adapted trace-guided baseline. Attack-vector shifts are particularly difficult: no configuration resolves more than 37.9% of these instances. Higher resolve rates are associated with a smaller share of missed-API failures and a larger share of incomplete executions among the remaining failures. In one configuration, withholding the reference PoC and its environment specification reduces resolve rate from 50.4% to 15.0%, highlighting the value of the supplied reference package. CrossPloit provides an execution-based measurement of under-reported exposure and of how far its enumeration can be automated.
items.author: Hung Nguyen-Huu, Nguyen Anh Tuan, Ting Zhang, Yue Liu, Chengran Yang, Lwin Khin Shar, Eng Lieh Ouh, David Lo

items.title: Towards Automated Recommendation of Steady-State Detection Algorithms for Software Performance Benchmarks
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16566v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Steady-state detection is a central step in software performance benchmarking, yet different detection methods rely on different assumptions and may perform best on different execution profiles. This paper formulates steady-state detection as an algorithm-recommendation problem: given a benchmark time series, predict which of two complementary detectors is more appropriate. The first, CP-SSD, identifies steady state through changepoint-based segmentation of the execution trace, whereas the second, KB-KSSD, uses a kernel-based approach to identify stable behaviour. We propose a data-driven recommender that characterises benchmark time series using automatically extracted features and combines supervised prediction with information derived from groups of time series exhibiting similar behaviour. The approach is evaluated on 407 labelled benchmark time series for which one of the two detectors can be identified as preferable with respect to a reference steady-state index. The proposed recommender selects the better detector correctly for 72.97% of the series, compared with 62.65% when always selecting the detector that performs best most often, corresponding to an absolute improvement of 10.32 percentage points. Paired statistical testing and bootstrap confidence intervals support this improvement. A comparison with a recommender using time-series features alone shows that the cluster-derived information mainly improves interpretability rather than predictive accuracy. Recommendations also remain highly stable when the unsupervised representation is learned from either the labelled subset or the full collection of 5,860 time series. These results demonstrate the feasibility of per-series steady-state detector recommendation while highlighting the need for broader labelled data, particularly for execution profiles favouring the changepoint-based detector.
items.author: Martin Beseda, Vittorio Cortellessa, Federico Di Menna, Daniele Di Pompeo, Luca Traini

items.title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16143v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Do large language model (LLM) migration agents learn from accumulated experience, or do apparent gains reflect retrieval and reference reuse? We evaluate an evidence-graded agent for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration across four studies. On 1,833 documentation-derived source-reference pairs, persistent memory improved reference conformity (RC) over a no-memory baseline by 0.015 [0.004, 0.025], while policy adaptation added no gain (-0.004 [-0.010, 0.001]). An audit found that 264 of 367 held-out units (72%) shared a PostgreSQL reference with training, and the memory effect on the 103 leak-free units fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011]. A model-free nearest-target copy baseline scored RC 0.222, outperforming all LLM systems (at most 0.163). A reference-grouped split reduced copying to 0.119; a rerun on 374 units in 118 independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect (0.005 [-0.003, 0.017]) and no policy effect. A separate Oracle-grounded evaluation on 216-224 real PL/SQL units showed that 10-22% of PostgreSQL-accepted units were behaviorally incorrect; a human-gated fix cycle increased demonstrably correct units from 98/216 to 167/224. A write-back study showed a 54% decline in retrieval margin as the knowledge base grew from 12 to 1,200 entries. We derive six evaluation rules that distinguish cross-task learning from reference leakage, copying, metric artifacts, and unstable feedback.
items.author: Oleg Grynets, Vasyl Lyashkevych, Valeriia Oliferuk, Vladyslav Babenko, Danylo Kovalchuk, Dmytro Kostetskyi

items.title: Beyond the Diff - VulSpot: A Vulnerability Dataset Where No Vulnerability Goes Unlocalized
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15737v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A vulnerability detector is only as trustworthy as the benchmark that scores it, and today's real-world datasets tend to flatter detectors. They are often built once and never refreshed, so they quickly miss new vulnerabilities, their labels are either noisy or heavily filtered, and their random splits let models train on near-copies of test code and on future vulnerabilities. Above all, when a fix only adds code, such as a missing NULL check, they do not point at where the vulnerability was, preventing detectors from learning to localize some of the most common C/C++ weaknesses. We present VulSpot, a living benchmark for detecting, classifying, and localizing vulnerabilities, with over 500k functions in 21 languages from 24k registered CVEs, including over 15k vulnerable C/C++ functions. By linking the code added by a patch to the existing statement it protects, VulSpot locates the vulnerability in 99.3\% of the functions that previous diff-based datasets used to leave without a location. Rather than discarding uncertain labels, it tells users how reliable each one is, and it comes with leak-free splits, complementary code context, and hierarchical CWE labels. An automated pipeline refreshes VulSpot every month, so that each release brings vulnerabilities no model has seen yet.
items.author: Dyna Soumhane Ouchebara, St\'ephane Dupont

items.title: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15316v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Building and evaluating security tools for IoT firmware requires targets whose weaknesses are known in ad- vance and can be reproduced in a running device. Two problems remain: (1) firmware collected from real-world products provides realistic software, but hardware dependencies and undocumented defects make it difficult to establish what a security tool should be expected to find; and (2) existing benchmarks typically collect sets of vulnerable or misconfigured firmware images without providing purpose-built vulnerable services with explicit weaknesses that a security analysis tool can target. We present IoTPwnBench, a synthetic, modular benchmark that brings these requirements together. IoTPwnBench contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles, including industrial controllers, health monitors, and household devices. Each vulnerable image runs a plausible device application with simulated sensors and actuators that generate live readings over its native interfaces while exposing one target weakness mapped to a primary CWE. A documented exploitation payload and observable signal establish the expected behavior independently of the evaluated tool. Every vulnerable image is paired with a corrected twin that preserves the device and service while removing that weakness. Researchers can therefore compare the same target before and after correction to assess detection and false positives for the target weakness. The benchmark produces kernel and filesystem binaries for static inspection and dynamic testing under QEMU. Device profiles and weakness modules remain separate, allowing the same scenario to be reused across device contexts. Vulnerable targets were validated manually, and the open source build workflow regenerates the firmware bit-for-bit.
items.author: Luca Ferrari, Marco Alecci, Luca Verderame, Jacques Klein, Francesco Pagano

items.title: Towards Runtime-Aware Observability for Java Virtual Threads
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.14999v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: OS-level observability tools join application requests to kernel events through the OS thread ID, assuming that a unit of work occupies one OS thread until it completes. Java virtual threads break this assumption: many virtual threads are multiplexed onto a few carrier threads, so a stable thread ID hides a changing unit of work, and the join fails silently. Existing virtual-thread-aware channels republish context or identity on every mount and unmount, and the JVMTI-based one pays this cost for the lifetime of the JVM, whether or not an observer is attached. We bind a 64-byte off-heap trace buffer to each virtual thread, at a fixed address for its lifetime, and publish the address to eBPF consumers through four USDT probes in a patched OpenJDK; a re-implemented JVMTI channel over the same buffer serves as a controlled comparison. The four-probe design attributed all 768 test markers correctly on both the content and the identity plane, while the naive two-probe design silently misattributes trace context. With no consumer attached, publication costs at most about 33 ns per transition; the remaining dormant cost is buffer allocation, about 0.37 microseconds per virtual thread, which is negligible on transition-heavy workloads but nearly doubles the cost of a creation-only microbenchmark. The JVMTI channel costs about 20% on transition-heavy workloads and about 1.8 microseconds per virtual thread on the creation-only one. We also show that, of the two update strategies OTEP 4947 permits, only in-place rewriting guarded by the record's valid flag is sound for readers that cache the record's address, as lifecycle-event readers do.
items.author: Wenjie Ding

items.title: Where LLM Agents Get Stuck Debugging Databases: Access More Than Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly asked not only to write code but to debug running systems from live runtime data. We report a field observation of one such agent (Claude Code) as it diagnosed eight database incidents in a production message-dispatch engine. In every incident whose root cause depended on runtime concurrency, the agent announced a cause, shipped a fix, and later walked it back, and each wrong guess cost a deploy-and-observe cycle. Mapping each incident to what the agent lacked, we find that access to production state was the most pervasive bottleneck. The missing access included live lock views, untruncated deadlock reports, read-only execution, and an explicit environment context. An access gap was present in all five concurrency-dependent incidents: alone in one, and in four combined with a reasoning error such as anchoring on an early cause, incomplete exploration of the configuration, or a misreading of the code's transaction semantics. The three incidents that did not depend on concurrency needed nothing beyond what the agent already had. Within the incidents, the agent's wrong hypotheses were consistent with the evidence it could see; they were not fabrications. We argue that the next step for production-debugging agents is a forensics layer that gives the agent the access it lacks inside existing security controls. Such a layer would combine a safe interrogation API, a lock-and-deadlock flight recorder, and a production replay harness.
items.author: Gustavo Pinto

items.title: Patterns for Designing CI/CD Workflows
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17276v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: CI/CD pipelines are difficult to build and maintain, and information about them is scattered across empirical studies, practitioner books, and catalogues of 'smells'. We collected candidate practices and anti-practices converted them into patterns, and then consolidated these into patterns. These patterns address issues such as security, pipeline scheduling, workflow structure, performance and failure and release management. Each pattern is contextualised and describes the problem it solves, the forces at play, the solution and the consequences.
items.author: Leandro Sousa, Filipe Correia

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16902v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.
items.author: Joseph G. Bronyah, Nasir U. Eisty

items.title: Rasoi: Visual Diffs for Evaluating Structural Changes Made by Coding Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16293v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents let developers modify software rapidly through natural language. However, as agents take on larger changes, developers can lose track of how the codebase is evolving. These edits may look correct on the surface while restructuring the system in unexpected ways: duplicating logic, changing modules outside the requested scope, removing functionality developers meant to keep, or introducing architectural drift. We investigate how visual diffs can help developers understand and evaluate the structural changes that coding agents make. We present Rasoi, a design probe that maps how a codebase's architecture evolves after each agent-made edit, letting developers inspect which architectural elements and relationships were added, modified, or removed across multiple levels of abstraction. We deployed Rasoi in a week-long study with 12 developers working on their own codebases across varied technical domains. We found that visual diffs helped developers see whether changes stayed within scope, notice unexpected restructuring, and understand how modified parts related to the system as a whole. Our findings suggest that the value of oversight tools for coding agents lies less in making developers trust the agent and more in helping developers feel confident in their own evaluation of agent-made changes. We discuss implications for visual tools that support code comprehension and human oversight in AI-assisted software development.
items.author: Riya Sahni, Aryan Kaul, Anushka Bhatnagar, Xuanming Zhang, Vivian Liu, Reya Vir, Lydia B. Chilton

items.title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.16116v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.
items.author: Vahid Haratian, Vahid Ansari, Mohammadhossein Malmir, Alois Knoll

items.title: Early Reflections on How Large Language Models are Reshaping Software Engineering Research
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are radically reshaping software engineering (SE) research. Yet, their steep financial and computational costs raise questions about who participates in that change, and who does not. By analysing all 1,918 papers published in the ICSE 2019-2026 Research and SEIP tracks, we uncover a shifting and highly concentrated research landscape. China and the US dominate LLM-based SE research, appearing in 74% of LLM-based publications between 2023-2026, yet they diverge sharply in their use of commercial versus open-weight models. Beneath this national dominance lies extreme institutional concentration: just 5 institutions in China and 7 in the US appear in more than half of their respective nations' LLM-based output. In the US, only half of the unique institutions active in 2023-2026 participated in LLM-based research, whereas Singapore displays broader usage, with 11 of 15 active institutions participating in LLM-based work. Furthermore, across 2023-2026 Research-track papers, industry involvement is more prevalent in LLM-based work (23.4% vs 16.9%), and academia-only papers make up a smaller share (63.4% vs 70.9%). Crucially, we expose a gap in model usage across industry and academia. SEIP track papers lean strongly towards commercial LLMs, with 77.4% featuring them and 40.5% using them exclusively. In contrast, only 21.2% of Research-track work relies strictly on commercial models, making greater use of open-weight models that typically support more sustainable and reproducible experiments. However, this divide warrants reflection on the extent to which SE research aligns with industry practice.
items.author: David Williams, Michail Kyrkos, Max Hort, Maria Kechagia, Justyna Petke, Federica Sarro

items.title: Does Confusing Code Confuse LLMs? A Pilot Study on C++
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15575v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for software maintenance tasks that depend heavily on code comprehension. While atoms of confusion, minimal code patterns empirically shown to impair human program comprehension, are well studied, it remains unclear whether these same patterns affect LLMs, and whether their impact varies across maintenance tasks. We present a pilot study evaluating the impact of atoms of confusion on LLM performance on C++ code drawn from three production libraries, using ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot on three software development tasks: atom injection and removal, output prediction, and code explanation. Our results reveal three preliminary findings: (i) the impact of atoms on LLMs is strongly task-dependent; (ii) atoms requiring reasoning about surrounding code are the most resistant to transformation, while localized syntactic atoms are handled reliably; and (iii) LLMs remove atoms of confusion more reliably than they inject them, suggesting that removal succeeds through pattern matching while injection requires deeper comprehension.
items.author: Tim van de Wetering, Lola Solovyeva, Fernando Castor

items.title: DafnyCert: Certifying Specification Strength in Dafny
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15548v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Formally verifying a method with Dafny guarantees correctness relative to its specification. However, a specification may be too permissive, allowing multiple outputs for the same input, even when the implementation produces only one. In this paper, we propose checkable certificates that provide independently verifiable evidence of whether a specification is weak or strong. A certificate of weakness contains an alternative implementation that verifies against the original specification, together with a witness input on which the original and alternative implementations produce different results. A certificate of strength is produced by constructing a harness around the original method such that successfully verifying the harness guarantees that the specification allows at most one possible output for any given input. We present DafnyCert, a tool that automatically produces these certificates. Strength is established by constructing and verifying the harness. Weakness is demonstrated by using the MutDafny mutation tool to find mutants that verify against the original specification, and by using the Hypothesis property-based testing framework to generate inputs that produce different outputs for the original program and the mutant. The resulting mutant and witness form a recheckable certificate of weakness. On a dataset of 3,910 verified Dafny methods from Dafny-Synthesis and VeriEquivBench, DafnyCert automatically certifies 3,570 methods (91.3%). We also provide certificates for the remaining 340 methods. To our knowledge, this is the first dataset in which every specification is backed by a checkable certificate of strength or weakness. These labels disagree with the benchmarks' original labels for 16.3% of the methods. These findings highlight the importance of supporting specification strength labels with independently checkable evidence.
items.author: \'Alvaro Silva, Isabel Amaral, Ruben Martins, Alexandra Mendes

items.title: Git2KG: Mining socio-technical relationships in GitHub repositories as temporal knowledge graphs
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15509v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The widespread use of Git and GitHub in open source software (OSS) projects has produced large volumes of data on collaborative software development. Existing approaches to mine those data often use graph models to (i) capture communication between developers in the issue tracker, or (ii) represent developer-developer co-authorship or developer-file code ownership networks from the editing history of code artifacts. Integrating these data in a single knowledge graph (KG) is complicated by the need to disambiguate authors and match entities from multiple sources. Moreover, most works using network analysis have taken a time-aggregated perspective that neglects temporal dynamics of collaborations. To address these issues, we present Git2KG, an extensible Python library that mines temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) from GitHub repositories. Git2KG extracts fine-grained co-editing relations and code ownership from the Git log. It further disambiguates developer identities to align the resulting graphs with management and communication networks extracted from GitHub issue trackers. Git2KG supports temporal analysis by slicing development events into fixed-size, non-overlapping time windows, yielding a series of knowledge graph snapshots per repository. It further supports computing node features and labels for downstream machine learning tasks. Snapshots can then be exported to PyTorch Geometric, PathPyG, and NetworkX for temporal network analysis, visualization, and graph learning.
items.author: Lennart Hessenauer, Lisi Qarkaxhija, Ingo Scholtes

items.title: KernelAudit: Contract-Aware Auditing of Validators for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15506v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The effectiveness of generating GPU kernels driven by a large language model (LLM) is highly dependent on the quality of the used validator (used to accept or reject a generated kernel candidate against the contracts of the given kernel-generation task), whose results inform reward assignment, candidate selection, and speedup claims during kernel generation. However, an existing validator suffers from various limitations, e.g., wrongly accepting a candidate due to missing its forbidden library use or wrongly rejecting a candidate due to determining its permitted library use as forbidden (constraints on library uses are stated in the task contracts).
  To assess the quality of a validator against the given task contracts, we propose an independent-audit approach for the validator by (1) construction of audit oracle: labeling a candidate as PASS or FAIL based on three separate dimensions in our proposed contract model (i.e., semantic correctness, implementation integrity, and measurement integrity) and (2) auditing of the validator against the audit oracle: comparing the labels of the candidate against the validation results produced by the validator. For semantic correctness, reference-calibrated stress tests check output correctness on valid inputs for a candidate. For implementation integrity, reference and candidate execution traces are used to determine specific library uses. For measurement integrity, timing checks assess whether the reported runtime reflects the full time needed to complete the candidate's computation. We apply our approach to assess the quality of six validators and 716 candidates from seven corpora, including constructed controls. The evaluation results show that our approach helps assess the existing six validators to have nontrivial false-reject rates. There is high-degree agreement between the candidate labels produced by our audit oracle and human judgments.
items.author: Ziyuan Li, Zihe Song, Xiaofang Qi, Wei Yang, Tao Xie

items.title: KernelMutate: Mutation-Guided Validation of Generated GPU Kernels
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15441v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generated GPU implementations are commonly accepted after a few differential tests, although replacement obligations may remain unchecked. We present KernelMutate, an empirical study of validation reliability using controlled faults, released implementations, and replacement tests. A five-draw anchor accepts 548 of 838 CUDA candidates. The full suite finds native FP32 witnesses for 136 accepted candidates and dtype-only findings for another 362, mostly low-precision execution limitations without established publisher guarantees. Source-guided testing identifies the full suite's 692 candidates at 26.1% lower charged cost, but yields only dtype evidence for 16 accepted candidates with native witnesses in the full suite. Independently observed context and boundary findings cover the same candidate set. Task-held-out template matching reveals differences in ranking and observation coverage: global top-eight recommendations match more probes than class-conditioned lists (51 versus 48 of 75), while conditional analyses restrict the apparent advantage at smaller limits. These template-matching results are offline measurements, not deployed-suite gains. Independent controls and replacement cases expose numerical-policy, binding, and custom-execution boundaries. Validation therefore needs to report witness domains and observation coverage alongside candidate yield and cost.
items.author: Ziyuan Li, Zihe Song, Shuxiao Xie, Mingfang Ji, Xiaofang Qi, Wei Yang, Tao Xie

items.title: AgentTorrent: A Dataset of Context and Harness Engineering Artifacts on GitHub
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.15436v1 Announce Type: new
