arXiv:2611.12544v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.
items.author: Paul H\"ausner, Jevgenija Rudzusika, Jens Sj\"olund, Ozan \"Oktem

items.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12466v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.
items.author: Zhaohui Xu, Xiaofei Xu, Doudou Zhou

items.title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12458v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.
items.author: Roger Guimer\`a, Kai-Hendrik Cohrs, Sergio Pedreira, Marta Sales-Pardo, Gustau Camps-Valls

items.title: AudioCodex: Streaming Autoencoders for Live Audio
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12375v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce AudioCodex, a fully causal autoencoder for live generative audio applications that compresses stereo audio into compact continuous latent sequences at ~10 Hz. It combines a Mean Flow magnitude autoencoder with latent hypersphere projection, bounded-noise augmentation, representation alignment, and adversarial phase recovery to learn representations that support both efficient downstream generation and high-quality reconstruction. Through extensive ablations, we show that AudioCodex outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of generation-reconstruction trade-off, whilst remaining strictly causal in both encoding and decoding. This work paves the way towards truly real-time interactive and streaming generative audio applications.
items.author: Marco Pasini, Javier Nistal, Cyran Aouameur, Stefan Lattner, George Fazekas

items.title: Tensor Network Kernel Machines for Nonlinear System Identification
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12326v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Over the past ten years Tensor Network Kernel Machines have enabled efficient nonlinear system identification through the use of low-rank tensor networks. The goal of this article is to provide the reader with a basic understanding of this model class in terms of its two defining properties. Furthermore, both the optimization and regularization of such models are discussed, together with recent developments and starting points for further exploration.
items.author: Kim Batselier

items.title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12319v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.
items.author: Junha Ryu, Hoi-Jun Yoo

items.title: Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks for Damage Identification in Ultrasonic Guided Wave Structural Health Monitoring
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12299v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Ultrasonic guided wave (UGW) inspection has become an effective method in structural health monitoring (SHM). While machine learning has enhanced damage detection capabilities, purely data-driven models remain constrained by extensive labeled datasets and limited physical interpretability. Standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) further suffer from spectral bias (F-Principle) in high-frequency regimes, prioritizing low-frequency components while failing to resolve the high-frequency oscillations critical for UGW reconstruction. Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks (PI-SIRENs) address these limitations by embedding governing partial differential equations directly into the training process. Building upon SIRENs, which utilize periodic activation functions to inherently capture high-frequency spectral content, the proposed framework is designed to operate effectively in sparse ultrasonic measurement regimes. This work introduces a frequency-domain PI-SIREN framework tailored for the Mindlin-Reissner plate theory to reconstruct ultrasonic wavefields without temporal discretization. The model parameters are optimized using a hybrid strategy comprising three phases: first-order Adam, residual-adaptive refinement (RAR) and quasi-Newton L-BFGS. Numerical and experimental evaluations confirm that the model serves as a physics-consistent baseline derived from sparse data, functioning as a computationally efficient surrogate for damage identification in SHM and non-destructive testing (NDT). Integrating the surrogate into a damage identification pipeline detects and localizes a milled notch from sparse experimental measurements with a localization error of 1 % of the plate diagonal. In contrast, data-driven benchmarks and MLPs with hyperbolic tangent activation functions, with and without Fourier feature embedding, are unable to identify damage due to higher reconstruction errors.
items.author: Lukas Jilke, Caspar Wasle, Norbert Hosters, Florian Raddatz, Marek Behr, Gerko Wende

items.title: Hierarchical Multi-Channel Tip-Over Prediction via Isolated Temporal Models for Planetary Rover Safety
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12261v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reliable tip-over prevention is critical for planetary rovers operating in unstructured environments where communication delays prevent real-time human intervention. Existing learning-based approaches typically optimize a single prediction objective, limiting their ability to capture both gradual instability evolution and abrupt terrain disturbances. This work presents a hierarchical multi-channel tip-over prediction framework based on isolated temporal learning. A multi-horizon Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) learns progressive instability patterns from inertial measurements, while a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based forward dynamics model predicts nominal rover motion and detects unexpected dynamic deviations through prediction residuals. These complementary signals are integrated through decision-level fusion and priority-based arbitration to generate graded safety actions, including early warning and emergency braking. The proposed system is deployed as an Orocos Real-Time Toolkit (RTT)-based safety component within the Rock robotics framework, operating at 100 Hz on a planetary rover software stack. Experiments on Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) samples collected across heterogeneous terrains demonstrate 97.58% event prediction coverage with a 1.82s median lead time, outperforming individual prediction channels. The results validate that isolated temporal models combined through hierarchical decision fusion provide a robust solution for real-time rover safety in uncertain terrain.
items.author: Siddhant Shete, Raul Dominguez, Frank Kirchner

items.title: CADMA: Capacity-Aware Coverage Decomposition for Generative Model Assessment
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12243v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Evaluating generative models requires measuring not only sample fidelity but also how well a generated set covers the real data distribution. Recent work has therefore introduced recall-oriented metrics for distribution-level evaluation. However, existing recall metrics often reduce distributional coverage to geometry-based coverage. This simplifying assumption weakens their diagnostic value and interpretability in two ways: these metrics provide only a single aggregate score that cannot distinguish essential diversity failures such as mode dropping and mode collapse, and geometry-based coverage can provide unreliable estimates by assigning high scores to poorly covered generative distributions. We therefore introduce CADMA, a capacity-aware framework for recall-oriented evaluation and diagnosis. CADMA evaluates distributional coverage through local capacity matching between real and generated samples, separating geometry-based coverage from effective coverage. This yields multi-dimensional coverage diagnostics that quantify mode dropping and mode collapse while reducing the overly optimistic estimates produced by geometry-based metrics. Through extensive experiments on toy data, real-world datasets, and generative models, we show that CADMA provides more reliable coverage estimates and more fine-grained, interpretable diagnostic signals of diversity failures than existing metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/Open-Debin/CADMA_NeurIPS2026.
items.author: Debin Meng, Zheng Gao, Ziquan Liu, Yanran Li, Ioannis Patras, Georgios Tzimiropoulos

items.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12240v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
items.author: Tomas Rasymas, Povilas Kvedaras

items.title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12225v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.
items.author: Jiantong Xu

items.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12162v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.
items.author: Lei Shu, Zizhou Huang, Yunuo Chen, Yifei Li, Tao Du, Minchen Li, Tuur Stuyck, Miles Macklin, Kui Wu, Bo Zhu, Yin Yang, Ming C. Lin, Alberta Longhini, Rika Antonova, Leonidas Guibas, Gordon Wetzstein, Jeannette Bohg, Chenfanfu Jiang

items.title: GPU-Accelerated Non-Interactive Encrypted Neural Network Training with Batched Diagonal Packing
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12161v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Training a neural network under homomorphic encryption requires transposes, batch reductions, optimizer updates, and repeated refreshes in addition to forward matrix products. We combine rectangular diagonal packing, feature-major SIMD mini-batch lanes, baby-step giant-step evaluation, and compact optimizer state in an MIT-licensed Rust CKKS implementation. Its CUDA path keeps training and bootstrap ciphertext arithmetic on the GPU, while retaining host key generation and client operations. In a matched 100-update experiment on the main non-interactive MNIST model, device-resident bootstrapping reduces training time from 14,268.295 to 293.075 seconds, a $48.68\times$ ratio against our CPU implementation, with exactly equal decoded parameters and predictions. Including setup and final evaluation gives a $40.67\times$ ratio. A separate GPU run completes ten passes over 4,800 images in 2,967.095 seconds and achieves 90.35% test accuracy versus 90.41% for its plaintext twin. These are single-initialization results; exact CPU/GPU parameter agreement is verified at 100 updates, not for the full 1,000-update run. Earlier completed CPU runs support a larger-batch key-switch advantage and baseline-batch accuracy within the registered tolerance, but the baseline-batch normalized key-switch target is missed. The released ReBoot baseline does not meet the common security-estimator threshold, and its full-setting CPU time is unmeasured. We therefore distinguish measured acceleration of our implementation from conditional layout comparisons and do not claim unconditional superiority over ReBoot.
items.author: Kentaro Mihara

items.title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12100v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. In this paper we first developed the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC) that unlike other life cycle models shifts the focus onto the forensic artifacts created during the life cycle of an AI system. Through FALC we derived a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation. Second, we collected examples for crimes with AI involvement throughout FALC and questions likely to be asked when investigating these crimes. Third, we propose a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise with a focus on the current possibility to analyze AI forensic artifacts using established techniques. For investigators, the model provides a systematic basis for identifying which artifacts to look for when an AI system is relevant to a case. For researchers, the classification shows where existing forensic methods already suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.
items.author: Adrian Johannes Staeves, Mayur Rattan Jaisinghani, Rebekah Overdorf, Frank Breitinger

items.title: BARS: Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis via Flow Matching
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12061v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We present BARS (Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis), a non-autoregressive rapping voice generation model based on Flow Matching, conditioned on a beat track (instrumental backing), lyrics, and a short reference voice for zero-shot timbre control. Unlike prior autoregressive rap synthesis, where rap pace and output duration are strictly determined by the beat, BARS enables independent control over the rap tempo, allowing flexible-length generation without explicit duration prediction or phoneme-level alignment. We encode lyrics using a pretrained ByT5 encoder with a lightweight Transformer adapter trained jointly with the model, without relying on speech-pretrained text encoders, enabling natural handling of non-standard orthography (e.g., slang, abbreviations) and numerals common in rap lyrics. To address alignment instabilities, such as token skipping or repetition, under strong beat conditioning, we propose Asymmetric Scaled RoPE for cross-attention, which introduces a positional structure to facilitate sequential lyric-audio alignment learning. Furthermore, the model supports partial re-generation via span masking, enabling lyric-level editing while preserving the surrounding vocal style. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high lyric fidelity, natural rap flow that is rhythmically coherent with the beat, and robust tempo control across a wide range of rapping styles and speeds.
items.author: Taemin Cho, Hector Martel, Enyan Koh

items.title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12059v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at $d$ coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a $\sqrt{d}$ dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from \emph{any} online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, $p$-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to $\sqrt{\log d}$ for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.
items.author: Tuo Liu, Edgar Dobriban, Francesco Orabona

items.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.12054v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.
items.author: Moritz Poguntke, Eda Oktay, Yuanzhe Xi, Erin Carson, Martin Stoll

items.title: MUTE: Multi-Level Alignment Uncoupling Against Talking-Head Exploitation for Voice Protection
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11989v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Talking-head generation models, which synthesize realistic facial animations from audio, are increasingly vulnerable to misuse in multimodal deepfake scenarios. Protecting such systems remains challenging, as talking-head models fundamentally rely on precise audio-visual alignment, while effective audio protection methods remain largely underexplored. In this work, we propose MUTE, an audio protection framework that uncouples the underlying audio-visual alignment through a multi-level strategy. Specifically, MUTE combines (1) Alignment-level Disruption, which directly perturbs cross-modal attention to disrupt structural alignment, and (2) Representation-level Degradation, which perturbs temporal audio embeddings to degrade their representations. To improve robustness, perturbations are constrained in the STFT domain to high-energy regions, making them resistant to post-processing, denoising, and adaptive attacks. An optional speaker-level objective further mitigates potential bypass via TTS-based resynthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MUTE consistently degrades lip synchronization across both white-box and black-box talking-head models while preserving perceptual audio quality. The proposed method remains effective under real-world transformations and can be combined with image-based approaches to provide stronger multimodal protection. The source code and project page are available at https://github.com/jindl465/MUTE.
items.author: Donghyun Kim, Jin Hong, Seungmin Kim, Dain Kim, Junseok Kwon, Daeseon Choi

items.title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11985v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.
items.author: Wei Chen, Lihao Zhuang, Yubing Wu, Delu Zeng

items.title: Beyond Prediction Residuals: Conformal Regret Calibration for Robust Contextual Linear Optimization
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11973v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Predict-then-optimize systems convert contextual forecasts into decisions, yet conformal robust optimization typically calibrates prediction residuals rather than downstream loss. For linear optimization, this parameter-space geometry can be badly misaligned with decision risk: large objective perturbations may preserve the optimizer, while small boundary-crossing perturbations may cause substantial regret. We introduce Conformal Regret Sets, a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that conformalizes an optimization-derived regret surrogate and uses its calibrated level set for minimax-regret refinement. We first show that directly conformalizing exact regret, although sufficient to certify the nominal predict-then-optimize decision, yields a degenerate robust problem: absent an exogenous bounded support, every alternative decision has unbounded worst-case regret. We therefore use SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret, as the conformal score, obtaining distribution-free finite-sample marginal regret guarantees under exchangeability. For contextual linear programs, the resulting set decomposes into polyhedral pieces aligned with the normal fan of the feasible polytope. A vertex is active if and only if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most half the calibrated threshold $\eta$, enabling local, output-sensitive generation of all relevant pieces. Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is the predicted gap to the closest competing vertex, the nominal and refined decisions admit the sharper worst-case-regret certificate $(\eta-2\Gamma)_+$, with an exact early exit when $\eta\leq 2\Gamma$. Experiments on contextual fractional knapsack validate the geometry and certificates: continuous refinement reduces the $0.95$-quantile and $\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.95}$ of regret by $9.1\%$ and $13.1\%$ relative to nominal PTO, while vertex-restricted refinement changes only $10.0\%$ of nominal decisions.
items.author: Lingjie Zhao, Hansheng Jiang, Wei Qi

items.title: Watching Itself Watch: Self-Auditing Visual Reliance for Video Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11949v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Video reasoning hinges on a small number of visually decisive tokens embedded in otherwise largely language-driven chains of thought. Yet prevailing post-training methods such as GRPO overlook this structure, assigning coarse trajectory-level rewards while requiring multiple rollouts and often costly external judges. We introduce Visually-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (VIOS), a post-training framework that identifies where a model under-utilizes visual evidence and concentrates learning at those positions. Our key insight is that a model can audit its own visual reliance: the divergence between its next-token distributions with and without the video reveals how strongly each prediction depends on the visual input. Measuring this reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged teacher exposes a per-token reliance gap, identifying positions where the teacher exploits visual evidence that the student overlooks. VIOS translates this signal into dense, targeted supervision through three complementary components: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher that co-evolves with the student, a contrastive objective that encourages predictions to depend on the video, and a reliance-gap gate that focuses learning on visually under-utilized tokens. Crucially, VIOS requires only a single on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers. Across 12 benchmarks spanning general, temporal, spatial, knowledge-intensive, and long-video understanding, VIOS consistently improves three model backbones and outperforms contemporary video-reasoning systems, while training in over 9x fewer steps, 60x fewer FLOPs, and 111x fewer generated tokens. Project page: https://vision.cs.utexas.edu/projects/VIOS/
items.author: Rohan Dugad, Mi Luo, Kristen Grauman

items.title: The Relative Value of Demonstration Data: Execution Time Limits and Operator Mixtures in Behavior Cloning
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11947v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Robot demonstration datasets combine demonstrations from teleoperators of uneven experience, so collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group match those from another. We measure this with a data multiple: the ratio of the numbers of demonstrations two groups need for their policies to reach the same success rate. On robomimic's simulated Square and Can tasks, we train behavior-cloning policies on demonstrations from the two teleoperators robomimic labels Better and the two it labels Worse, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations. On Square, within robomimic's 25-second time limit, an all-Worse training set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. Most of this difference is late completion: policies trained on Worse demonstrations finish later, as the Worse teleoperators do, and with a 100-second limit the multiple falls to 1.11. On Can, most of the difference remains at 100 seconds. If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.
items.author: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Youran Sun, Jingxin Yang, Kejia Zhang, Haizhao Yang

items.title: AI-Driven Discovery of Entanglement Witness in Spin Hamiltonians
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11935v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Entanglement is a crucial resource in quantum science and engineering, but detecting it in many-body states from experimentally accessible observables remains challenging. Here we introduce EntNet, an AI-driven framework to discover compact combinations of spin observables that accurately distinguish entangled from fully separable many-body mixed states in one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ chains governed by short-range Hamiltonians. We construct local-unitary-invariant representations of measurable Pauli correlators up to four-body order, sparsely select 16 candidate invariant feature channels, and learn their spatial structure using a Transformer architecture with rotary positional embeddings. Using only expectation values of these low-order observables, EntNet achieves $>98\%$ recall on certified entangled states with near-zero false-positive rates on separable states. Remarkably, it exhibits transferability across system sizes and distinct Hamiltonian families, including frustrated and disordered spin models, with minimal loss of accuracy. Beyond detection, EntNet provides physical insight into entanglement detection by revealing a selective spatial organization of pair correlations, while its finite-temperature decision boundary tracks the excitation gap of Jordan-Wigner quasiparticles. These results establish a transferable and physically interpretable framework for data-driven discovery of entanglement witnesses from local correlation functions.
items.author: Jiwei Tian, Mouyang Cheng, Mingda Li

items.title: RBA: A Read-out Basis Adapter for Parameter-Efficient Interactive OCTA Vessel Segmentation with SEEM
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11906v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Retinal disease monitoring with optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) relies on segmentation of vessels and the foveal avascular zone (FAZ). Promptable models such as SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) allow click-based refinement, but without adaptation SEEM segments thin vessels poorly and needs many clicks. Fully fine-tuning its 342 million parameters on a few hundred images is costly and risks overfitting, and parameter-efficient methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) usually adapt only the encoder. Yet SEEM reads every candidate mask from one feature map at quarter resolution, too coarse for vessels one to three pixels wide. This study introduces the Read-out Basis Adapter (RBA), whose read-out branch generates 32 image-specific basis maps at half resolution. Each candidate accesses them through its own vector and a zero-initialised projection, so the model starts exactly as SEEM. The encoder branch, a standard rank-1 LoRA, supplies the information needed to tell arteries from veins. RBA adds 0.47 million trainable parameters. Under simulated error-driven clicks, with the ground truth used only to place them, RBA outperforms LoRA, Conv-LoRA andAdaptFormer on OCTA-500 3mmlarge vessels. Averaged over three seeds, it reaches an intersection over union (IoU) of 85.16% and a Dice score of 91.93%, 2.90 and 1.72 percentage points above Conv-LoRA. On the 6 mm subset, one run gives margins of 4.35 and 2.76 points. The gain extends to arteries, veins and ROSE-O but not to the FAZ. In SEEM, adaptation capacity pays more at the mask read-out than in the encoder.
items.author: Jaafar M. Al-Ghabban, Mohammad Reza Mohammadi

items.title: How Far Must a Test Explore? Certifying Composable Read-Write Interfaces from Their Own Random Edits
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11899v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Random tests of stateful code check laws, like reading back a written value, at states that random writes reach. The laws hold at every state exactly when the code behaves like a record with hidden data, so a pass is taken as evidence. This can fail: the laws can hold at every sample while the code is far from any record. The laws are local, but behaving like a record is global. Self-testing and stability theorems bridge this gap when the query distribution is controlled by the tester or preserved by the tested maps, but here it is generated by the tested writes, which need not be invertible.
  We ask how far a test must explore. An interface has $m$ binary variables, each with a read and two writes; in a record, reads return their bits and writes set only their bits. Samples are the ends of geometric runs of mean $\ell$ of uniformly random writes from a start distribution; a tester adds its own write chains of depth $d$. The distance is the least, over records with hidden data, of the largest probability that a read or write differs from it at a sample.
  From one start state, law checks at $O(m^2\log m/\epsilon)$ samples certify, at fixed confidence, any threshold $\epsilon$ after geometric runs of every positive mean, while runs of fixed positive length can pass at distance $1/2$. For the worst start distribution, take $\epsilon=m^{-\beta}$ with fixed $0<\beta\le1$. For $d\le cm$ with fixed $c<1/2$, a polynomial budget of samples and writes exists exactly when $\ell=\Omega(m)$, where law checks suffice. With no runs, the least depth for this budget is $(1/2+o(1))m$. Counting samples alone, in the worst case at $\epsilon=1/(32m)$ and $d\le m/16$, the critical mean for a polynomial budget is $\Theta(m\log(m/d)/\log m)$, by exhaustive search. So one start state needs only law checks, and the worst case at these thresholds needs exploration linear in $m$ if writes are counted.
items.author: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Jingxin Yang, Youran Sun, Haizhao Yang

items.title: Your Company Has No Model of Itself. Agents Can Build One - Joao Wenzel, Citadel Securities
items.summary:
Every company has someone who knows everything: the reorgs, the politics, which projects are really on track. Joao Wenzel of Citadel Securities explains how his team approximates that person with an agentic system that builds an institutional memory from decks, Slack, meeting notes, code changes and agent traces. Borrowing the idea of a state estimator from robotics, the system updates its beliefs as evidence arrives, lets facts age, grades its own predictions against what actually happened, and takes corrections from people. He shows why simple retrieval isn't enough, how agents catch "watermelon projects" that are green on the outside and red on the inside, and how back-testing showed that projects the agent flagged were twice as likely to slip.

Anirudh Veeraragavan, lead security engineer at Fieldguide, argues that in finance an agent getting the right answer isn't enough; you have to be able to show how it got there. items.title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
items.summary:
1. Introduction
  2. Performance and efficiency

  5. Science and engineering

November 9, 2026

Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

  1. [1]Introduction
  2. [2]Performance and efficiency
  3. [3]Science and engineering
  4. [4]Safety and alignment
  5. [5]Availability

We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.

Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.

We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.

When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:

Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.

Agentic coding: FrontierCode 2.0Agentic search: WANDRHardware engineering: BenchCAD 2.1Multidisciplinary reasoning: Humanity’s Last ExamVisual chart recognition: Chartography

Coding

Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.

As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

Cybersecurity

Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²

Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program, which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.

We built our Code Guardian harness with Mythos 5.1, and we’d switch to Mythos 5.2 to give our customers more powerful cyber capabilities.”

Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns.”

Science and engineering

Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.

Theoretical physics

Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.

Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.

Protein folding

Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.

Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:

Dyno TherapeuticsColumbia UniversityBiohub

We are excited to help Anthropic push the reasoning capabilities further to reduce the cost of designing capsids overall.”

Claude’s approach cleverly tackles this problem for symmetric assemblies, making it possible for individual scientists to model systems on personal workstations that would otherwise require dedicated clusters.”

We will continue to incorporate such contributions from the community that extend our tools to important application domains.”

Mathematics

Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.

Read more about the formalization here.

Hardware and robotics

Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.

Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.

Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here.

Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.

Research and analysis

Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.

Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2:

Safety and alignment

No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.

Alignment testing

We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).

We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵

We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).

We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.

The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.

Safeguards

Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.

AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.

Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report, which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.

We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features).

Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards

Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe.

Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form. Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

Availability

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform.

This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here.

Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program. Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security, powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program.

Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs.

Footnotes

1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities.

2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card).

3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus, EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension, SymProFold, CapBuild, MoLPC, CombFold, Uni-Fold Symmetry, Apodex Discovery, and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 (PDB:1LP3). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2.

4 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication.

5 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards.

items.author: Olivia Stoner

items.title: Fade to... Red? Scheduling Coloured Noise Exploration Supports Efficient Robot Learning with Reduced Movement Jerk
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11868v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control is commonly driven by temporally uncorrelated Gaussian (white) action noise, which leads to jerky motions with locally constrained exploration. In contrast, temporally correlated coloured noise, particularly pink noise, has been shown to support more efficient exploration in RL. Motivated by these findings, we inquire whether scheduling changes to the noise colour over the course of training can outperform white noise for continuous control robotics. We perform a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, together with generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks with a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand. We find that the noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or end performance, whereas fading towards red noise halves the jerk of exploration in every task. Balancing learning efficiency, end performance and smoothness, red noise emerges as the preferred strategy: it learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less movement jerk. We therefore recommend exploration schedulers that fade towards red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.
items.author: Francisco M. L\'{o}pez, Francisco Cruz

items.title: DeFSM: Robust and Efficient Decentralization of Federated Submodular Maximization
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11866v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Submodular maximization seeks a small subset best representing a large dataset. In its federated setting, the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine. Removing the server raises a trilemma of decentraliza- tion, efficiency, and security. We propose DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient architecture that replaces the server with a lightweight smart contract and a pool of independent, consensus-free agents. Its aggregation rule, SafeGM, builds on two notions from combinatorial geometry: Tukey depth and safe points (the points lying in the convex hull of the good points wherever the bad points are). SafeGM makes the robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections, which the contract can compute efficiently, and lifts it back as a convex combination of actual updates. Since lifting loses information, it uses the projected geometric median only when its depth certifies it, and otherwise a Tukey median. The share of bad updates is then bounded only by a count: how many there are, not what they contain. We prove, and confirm empirically, that this bound controls the solution quality. On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST, with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and retains on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal reference, the geometric median at a trusted central server. The geometric median decentralized in its best setting would retain about 96%, but the contract cannot compute it, and so each agent would have to download six times more data, or each client twice as much.
items.author: Duc A. Tran, Dung Truong, Duy Le

items.title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11861v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. As of Fall 2026, human red-teaming may be nearing saturation, especially on the Gemini family of models. In this work, we argue that despite this apparent plateau, prompt injection attacks are still possible and continued effort into prompt injection defense is needed.
  We design a new synthetic evaluation dataset which uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals. Such dataset design helps us to evaluate prompt injection robustness as a model ability to respect instruction hierarchy, and disentangle this ability from model knowledge of security practices. We show that an agentic attacker of increased capabilities can reliably trick model to follow instructions in tool output in our evaluation, even for models previously considered robust on public prompt injection benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena. This shows that current frontier defenses may require proactive, automated red-teaming to remain resilient to increasingly capable adversaries.
items.author: Alexey Kurakin, Vishal Karande, Alex Bie, Chongyang Shi, Shuang Song, Saeed Mahloujifar, Abdullatif K\"oksal, Jamie Hayes, Juliette Pluto, Yinghao Sun, Kamalika Chaudhuri

items.title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11805v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.
items.author: Lianghao Cao, George Stepaniants, Andrew M. Stuart

items.title: ChemInsight: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating and Diagnosing Chemistry Understanding and Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11794v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce ChemInsight, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on chemistry tasks that require multi-step reasoning and structured chemical understanding. We propose a two-dimensional scoring system (scope and depth) to assess both task coverage and reasoning completeness. ChemInsight consists of 203 challenging chemistry questions organized into 50 bundles, which support the two-dimensional scoring evaluation scheme.
  We evaluate ten representative LLMs using ChemInsight and observe consistently low performance across models, with scope scores below 30% and depth scores below 11%, substantially lower than human expert performance. We then proceed to ask (1) What factor limits the advancement of current LLMs in chemistry? (2) To what extent are statistically driven language-model training methods effective at modeling chemistry symbolic language such as SMILES? And (3) Can LLM performance in chemistry be improved through intensive training on large, domain-specific corpora?
items.author: Changyu Hu, Yiming Zou, Xin Tang, Yiru Pan, Zicheng Huang, Deng Zhao, Qing Cui, Zhenduo Zhang, Wang Ren, Xiao Li

items.title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.11780v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
